character.centerRule: God remains the center only where the bounded source materially identifies divine speech, action, presence, relation, or remembered interpretation. Titles and metaphors do not erase speaker, genre, sequence, or evidence limits.

phases.orientation: God creates, addresses human beings, judges violence, preserves life, and limits human ambition.
phases.title: Maker and the early world

phases.orientation: God calls, promises, tests, meets, wrestles, and works through family histories.
phases.title: Promise and the patriarchs

phases.orientation: God names himself, hears Israel, confronts Egypt, gives covenant words, and discloses mercy and judgment.
phases.title: Name and deliverance

phases.orientation: Glory, holiness, atonement, blessing, Spirit, rebellion, and loyalty shape life near God.
phases.title: Presence in the wilderness

phases.orientation: God accompanies Israel, speaks through prophets, answers prayer, and challenges royal power.
phases.title: Land, judges, and kings

phases.orientation: Foreigners, empires, heavenly assemblies, wisdom, judgment, and mercy widen the field.
phases.title: Judgment, exile, and the nations

phases.orientation: Poetry speaks to and about God through praise, grief, confession, trust, knowledge, and time.
phases.title: Prayer and wisdom

phases.orientation: Prophets encounter holiness, announce judgment, name God’s purposes, and hold out renewal.
phases.title: The prophetic voice

phases.orientation: Spirit, kingship, compassion, justice, waiting, restoration, and divine constancy face the future.
phases.title: Future and faithfulness

phases.orientation: Jesus’ birth, prayer, teaching, suffering, commission, and the Word reshape how God is named.
phases.title: Jesus names the Father

phases.orientation: John’s Gospel and Pentecost press on sending, authority, unity, seeing, worship, prayer, and Spirit.
phases.title: Jesus and God

phases.orientation: Apostolic speech and final vision hold creation, judgment, Christ, love, and God’s dwelling together.
phases.title: Apostolic witness and the end

character.throughline: The trail moves from creation and early judgment through covenant, exodus, dwelling, kingship, wisdom, prophecy, Jesus’ witness to the Father, apostolic claims about Father, Son, and Spirit, and the final vision of God dwelling with humanity.

leftEvidence.title: God creates and speaks light

points.label: Divine action
points.left: God creates the heavens and earth, speaks light into darkness, and names day and night.
points.right: God deliberates, makes humankind in the divine image, blesses them, and gives them rule and food.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Light appears because God speaks; the text reports no struggle with another maker.
points.right: Male and female receive the image, blessing, and a shared commission.

compares.posture: The two creation scenes move from God’s ordering speech to the human vocation created within that ordered world.

rightEvidence.title: God makes humanity in God’s image

compares.tension: God alone creates, while humans receive a derived image and delegated rule.
compares.title: Creator and image bearers

leftEvidence.title: God forms and plants

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The LORD God forms the man from dust, breathes life, plants a garden, and causes trees to grow.
points.right: God calls to the hiding humans, questions them, announces consequences, clothes them, and bars the tree of life.

points.label: Human response
points.left: The human receives life and place before receiving the later command.
points.right: The humans hide, accuse, receive garments, and leave the garden.

compares.posture: The planted place is first given as life-giving provision and later guarded after human disobedience.

rightEvidence.title: God seeks, questions, judges, and clothes

compares.tension: The same God gives breath and trees, then clothes the humans and bars access to the tree of life.
compares.title: Gifted garden and guarded garden

leftEvidence.title: God warns Cain and hears blood

points.label: Divine action
points.left: God questions Cain, warns about sin, names Abel’s blood as a witness, judges Cain, and marks him against vengeance.
points.right: God sees pervasive evil, grieves, announces destruction, and gives Noah detailed instructions for preservation.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Cain is angry, kills Abel, denies responsibility, protests, and departs.
points.right: Noah finds favor and does what God commands while the wider earth is described as corrupt.

compares.posture: Cain’s murder and the flood generation show divine attention to bloodshed at personal and world scale.

rightEvidence.title: God grieves violence and preserves Noah

compares.tension: Cain receives judgment and protection; the corrupt earth receives judgment through the flood with one family preserved.
compares.title: Violence seen in one life and in the earth

leftEvidence.title: God limits judgment and sets the bow

points.label: Divine action
points.left: God receives Noah’s offering, promises not to strike every living thing again, blesses life, and gives the rainbow as covenant sign.
points.right: The LORD comes down, assesses the city and tower, confuses speech, and scatters the builders.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Noah builds an altar; humanity receives commands concerning life and blood.
points.right: Human beings seek a name and security through one city; their shared project stops.

compares.posture: The post-flood covenant secures creation’s continuance, while Babel shows that preservation does not remove divine judgment of human ambition.

rightEvidence.title: God descends and scatters Babel

compares.tension: God promises not to repeat the flood yet still intervenes against a unified city project.
compares.title: A preserved earth and a scattered city

leftEvidence.title: God calls Abram away

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The LORD commands Abram to leave and promises land, nation, blessing, and a wider blessing through him.
points.right: God answers Abram’s fear and childlessness, counts faith as righteousness, and binds the land promise through a covenant sign.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Abram goes, enters Canaan, builds altars, and calls on the LORD’s name.
points.right: Abram questions, believes, prepares the animals, falls into deep sleep, and receives a future history.

compares.posture: The initial call promises blessing; the later vision specifies descendants, land, delay, and affliction.

rightEvidence.title: God promises descendants and land

compares.tension: A broad promise to bless the families of earth develops through one family’s long and painful future.
compares.title: Called blessing and delayed covenant

leftEvidence.title: God names covenant and sign

points.label: Divine action
points.left: God identifies himself as God Almighty, renames Abram, promises descendants and land, and commands circumcision.
points.right: The LORD chooses to disclose the outcry against Sodom and allows Abraham’s repeated appeal concerning the righteous and wicked.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Abraham must walk before God; every male in the household receives the sign.
points.right: Abraham approaches, asks about justice, and presses the number down to ten.

compares.posture: One scene marks Abraham’s household; the other lets Abraham question how the Judge of all the earth treats righteous and wicked.

rightEvidence.title: God discloses judgment to Abraham

compares.tension: Belonging is marked bodily, while justice is explored through sustained dialogue.
compares.title: Covenant sign and covenant justice

leftEvidence.title: God tests Abraham over Isaac

points.label: Divine action
points.left: God commands the offering of Isaac, stops Abraham’s hand, provides a ram, and renews the promise.
points.right: The LORD stands above the stairway, repeats the ancestral promise, and promises presence and return.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Abraham obeys; Isaac asks about the lamb; the angel interrupts the act.
points.right: Jacob wakes afraid, names the place, sets a stone, and makes a conditional vow.

compares.posture: The Isaac test threatens the promised line; Jacob’s dream renews the promise to a fugitive descendant.

rightEvidence.title: God meets Jacob in flight

compares.tension: God tests one bearer of promise and assures another without explaining why their encounters differ so sharply.
compares.title: The threatened promise and promised presence

leftEvidence.title: God meets Jacob in struggle

points.label: Divine action
points.left: A mysterious man wrestles Jacob, wounds him, renames him Israel, and blesses him.
points.right: Joseph distinguishes his brothers’ evil intention from God’s intention to preserve many lives.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Jacob refuses release without blessing and says he has seen God face to face.
points.right: The brothers fear revenge; Joseph refuses God’s place and comforts them.

compares.posture: Jacob names a direct, wounding encounter with God; Joseph names God’s purpose within human actions across years.

rightEvidence.title: Joseph names God’s purpose in human evil

compares.tension: One scene is immediate and mysterious; the other interprets providence after events have unfolded.
compares.title: God in struggle and behind survival

leftEvidence.title: God hears and names himself

points.label: Divine action
points.left: God appears in fire, declares Israel’s suffering seen and heard, commissions Moses, and gives the name tied to “I AM.”
points.right: God names himself as the LORD and promises to bring out, redeem, take Israel as a people, and bring them into the land.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Moses turns aside, hides his face, objects, and asks what name to give Israel.
points.right: Israel is addressed as a people who will know the LORD through deliverance.

compares.posture: Moses receives the divine name at the bush; Israel receives a chain of actions through which that name will be known.

rightEvidence.title: God links the name to covenant action

compares.tension: The name is spoken before deliverance and then tied to what God promises to do.
compares.title: The disclosed name and promised acts

leftEvidence.title: God passes through Egypt

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The LORD strikes Egypt’s firstborn while the marked Israelite houses are passed over.
points.right: The LORD commands movement, divides the sea, protects Israel, throws Egypt into confusion, and returns the waters.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Israel marks doors and stays inside; Pharaoh summons Moses and releases the people.
points.right: Israel fears, crosses on dry ground, sees the Egyptians dead, and trusts the LORD.

compares.posture: The two scenes preserve distinct acts of deliverance from the same Egyptian crisis.

rightEvidence.title: God makes a path through the sea

compares.tension: One protects marked houses amid death; the other opens a public path and closes it over pursuers.
compares.title: Rescue through blood and through water

leftEvidence.title: God descends on Sinai

points.label: Divine action
points.left: God names Israel a treasured possession and priestly kingdom, sets boundaries, and descends in fire, cloud, sound, and trembling.
points.right: God identifies himself as deliverer, forbids rival gods and images, and orders worship, time, family, life, marriage, property, speech, and desire.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Israel agrees, consecrates, waits, and must not cross the boundary.
points.right: The people tremble and stand far off while Moses approaches the darkness.

compares.posture: The mountain appearance prepares for the direct covenant words that follow.

rightEvidence.title: God speaks covenant commands

compares.tension: Dangerous nearness and moral instruction belong together, yet the people end at a distance.
compares.title: God descends and God speaks

leftEvidence.title: God threatens judgment and relents

points.label: Divine action
points.left: God tells Moses of Israel’s corruption, announces consuming wrath, and relents after Moses appeals to reputation and promise.
points.right: The LORD passes before Moses and proclaims mercy, grace, patience, covenant love, faithfulness, forgiveness, and judgment.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Israel makes and worships the calf; Moses intercedes before seeing the camp.
points.right: Moses bows, asks for presence, pardon, and inheritance for a stiff-necked people.

compares.posture: Moses’ appeal after the calf is followed by God’s own proclamation of mercy, faithfulness, forgiveness, and judgment.

rightEvidence.title: God proclaims the divine name and character

compares.tension: The narrative says God relents; the proclamation refuses to reduce mercy to the absence of accountability.
compares.title: Intercession and the proclaimed character

leftEvidence.title: Glory fills the tabernacle

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The cloud covers the tent, the LORD’s glory fills it, and the cloud or fire directs Israel’s journeys.
points.right: The LORD’s glory appears and fire consumes the offering on the altar.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Even Moses cannot enter when the glory fills the dwelling.
points.right: The people shout and fall on their faces.

compares.posture: The completed dwelling is filled by glory, and priestly service culminates in fire from before the LORD.

rightEvidence.title: Fire comes from before the LORD

compares.tension: Both signs confirm presence while also producing distance, awe, and bodily response.
compares.title: Presence that fills and fire that accepts

leftEvidence.title: God provides guarded approach and removal

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The LORD regulates Aaron’s entrance, offerings, incense, blood, and the two goats for atonement and removal of sins.
points.right: The LORD gives words by which priests place the divine name on Israel: blessing, keeping, light, grace, attention, and peace.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Aaron approaches only as commanded; one goat is killed and one bears sins away.
points.right: Aaron and his sons speak the blessing; Israel receives the named favor.

compares.posture: Atonement regulates entrance and removal of sin; blessing places God’s name and peace on the people.

rightEvidence.title: God places the name in blessing

compares.tension: The people are brought near through priestly mediation that includes both costly cleansing and generous speech.
compares.title: Guarded approach and named blessing

leftEvidence.title: God shares the Spirit among elders

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The LORD takes from the Spirit on Moses and places it on seventy elders, including two who remain in the camp.
points.right: The LORD charges Israel with unbelief, threatens destruction, hears Moses’ appeal, pardons, and still bars the rebellious generation from the land.

points.label: Human response
points.left: The elders prophesy; Joshua objects; Moses wishes all the LORD’s people had the Spirit.
points.right: Moses appeals to the nations and God’s self-proclaimed character; Caleb is distinguished.

compares.posture: God supplies leadership through the Spirit and later confronts a people who refuse trust despite signs.

rightEvidence.title: God judges unbelief and hears intercession

compares.tension: Divine provision widens participation, while persistent unbelief still brings consequence after pardon.
compares.title: Shared Spirit and resisted presence

leftEvidence.title: God gives water and judges leaders

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The LORD instructs Moses to speak to the rock, gives water, and says Moses and Aaron failed to believe and sanctify him.
points.right: The command names the LORD as Israel’s God, calls for whole-person love, and places the words through daily life.

points.label: Human response
points.left: The people contend; Moses speaks harshly and strikes twice; the congregation drinks.
points.right: Israel must hear, love, remember, teach, speak, bind, and write.

compares.posture: Meribah identifies leaders who fail to sanctify God; the Shema calls the whole people to exclusive love and remembered words.

rightEvidence.title: Israel hears that the LORD is one

compares.tension: God gives water even as leaders fail, while covenant loyalty is framed as a daily whole-life response.
compares.title: Failed sanctification and whole-person love

leftEvidence.title: God commissions Joshua

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The LORD promises presence, land, and success tied to courage and careful attention to the instruction.
points.right: The LORD’s anger gives Israel into enemies, mercy raises judges, and judgment tests the nations when Israel repeatedly turns away.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Joshua must cross, lead, meditate, obey, and refuse fear.
points.right: Israel serves, forgets, cries under oppression, follows judges briefly, and becomes more corrupt after they die.

compares.posture: Joshua begins with assurance tied to instruction; Judges narrates repeated abandonment after that generation.

rightEvidence.title: God responds to Israel’s recurring abandonment

compares.tension: God’s presence and covenant words remain, while Israel’s response cycles through forgetting, oppression, and rescue.
compares.title: Promised presence and recurring abandonment

leftEvidence.title: God calls Samuel in a time of rare words

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The LORD calls Samuel, confirms judgment on Eli’s house, and establishes Samuel as a trustworthy prophet.
points.right: The LORD tells Samuel that Israel has rejected divine kingship, orders a warning, and finally tells him to appoint a king.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Samuel initially mistakes the voice, learns to answer, fears to report, and tells Eli everything.
points.right: The elders demand a king like the nations and refuse the warning about royal taking.

compares.posture: Samuel becomes a prophet through hearing God, then later hears Israel demand visible rule like the nations.

rightEvidence.title: God interprets Israel’s demand for a king

compares.tension: God establishes prophetic speech and also permits a kingship request named as rejection.
compares.title: A heard voice and a demanded king

leftEvidence.title: God refuses David’s house and promises one

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The LORD recalls moving in a tent, rejects David’s proposed temple role, and promises David a house, son, kingdom, and enduring throne.
points.right: Solomon praises covenant faithfulness and asks God to hear prayers directed toward the temple across sin, defeat, drought, exile, and foreign prayer.

points.label: Human response
points.left: David desires to build; Nathan first agrees, then carries the corrected word.
points.right: The king kneels and appeals for Israel, foreigners, and future exiles.

compares.posture: The promise to David reverses his building plan; Solomon later prays at the completed temple without confining God there.

rightEvidence.title: Solomon addresses the God heaven cannot contain

compares.tension: Dynasty and sanctuary are both connected to God yet neither becomes possession or containment.
compares.title: God promises a house and hears from a house

leftEvidence.title: God answers Elijah by fire

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The LORD answers Elijah’s prayer with fire that consumes offering, wood, stones, dust, and water.
points.right: The LORD questions Elijah, passes by amid wind, earthquake, and fire, speaks in a low sound, and gives new assignments and a preserved remnant.

points.label: Human response
points.left: The people waver, watch the failed Baal appeal, fall down, confess, and seize the prophets.
points.right: Elijah repeats his complaint and receives work, successors, judgment, and correction of his isolation.

compares.posture: Carmel gives a public answer by fire; Horeb corrects Elijah through a quieter encounter and a hidden remnant.

rightEvidence.title: God questions Elijah and speaks after the storm

compares.tension: God’s action is unmistakable in one scene and easily overlooked in the other.
compares.title: Fire before the nation and a quiet word to Elijah

leftEvidence.title: God heals a foreign commander

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The God of Israel heals Naaman through Elisha’s simple instruction and receives the foreigner’s confession.
points.right: The LORD is addressed as creator and enthroned God, answers the Assyrian boast, promises Jerusalem’s deliverance, and strikes the camp.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Naaman resists, washes, is restored, refuses other gods, and asks mercy for a compromised public duty.
points.right: Hezekiah spreads the letter in prayer; Isaiah delivers the answer; Sennacherib returns home.

compares.posture: Naaman comes to confess Israel’s God through healing; Assyria’s king mocks that God and is driven back.

rightEvidence.title: God answers Assyria’s challenge

compares.tension: Nations encounter God through mercy in one scene and judgment in the other.
compares.title: God known by a foreigner and challenged by an empire

leftEvidence.title: God warns, judges, and stirs return

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The God of the ancestors repeatedly sends messengers, gives the people over after sustained rejection, and later stirs Cyrus to rebuild.
points.right: God commends Job and sets limits on the accuser’s power while permitting devastating loss.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Leaders mock messengers, the city falls, survivors go into exile, and a Persian king issues a return decree.
points.right: The accuser challenges Job’s motives; raiders and fire take property and children; Job grieves and worships.

compares.posture: Chronicles explains exile through rejected messengers; Job’s losses begin through a heavenly exchange hidden from the sufferer.

rightEvidence.title: God permits Job’s testing in the heavenly court

compares.tension: One history gives a moral sequence; the other denies the sufferer access to the scene behind his pain.
compares.title: Public judgment and hidden heavenly permission

leftEvidence.title: God answers Job from the whirlwind

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The LORD questions Job about earth, sea, dawn, death, and the world’s breadth rather than first explaining Job’s suffering.
points.right: God stands in an assembly, rebukes unjust rulers called gods, and announces that they will die like humans.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Job is addressed as a challenger whose knowledge is limited.
points.right: The judged figures favor the wicked and fail to defend weak people; the psalm ends by asking God to judge the earth.

compares.posture: Job 38 displays divine knowledge through creation questions; Psalm 82 displays divine authority through judgment of exalted rulers.

rightEvidence.title: God judges in the divine assembly

compares.tension: God’s unmatched perspective does not remove the demand that delegated powers practice justice.
compares.title: The Creator questions Job and judges the assembly

leftEvidence.title: God’s power is described through measure and mercy

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The writer says God can act with great power yet orders all things by measure and shows mercy because all belong to God.
points.right: The sage says human speech cannot finish naming God, whose works exceed praise and whose greatness is beyond tracing.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Creatures are described as small before God and corrected little by little so they may turn from wickedness.
points.right: The readers are urged to exalt God while admitting that their language falls short.

compares.posture: Wisdom describes powerful mercy through God’s care for creatures; Sirach says speech cannot finish naming God’s greatness.

rightEvidence.title: Praise reaches the limit of speech

compares.tension: Specific claims about mercy coexist with confession that God exceeds human praise.
compares.title: Measured mercy and praise beyond speech

leftEvidence.title: God’s majesty and human vocation

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The psalm addresses the LORD’s majestic name, recalls the heavens as divine work, and marvels that God remembers and appoints humans.
points.right: The heavens declare God’s glory without audible speech, while the LORD’s instruction speaks clearly, restores, warns, and exposes hidden faults.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Weak human beings receive honor and rule beneath God’s rule.
points.right: The speaker moves from observing creation to desiring cleansed words and thoughts.

compares.posture: Psalm 8 asks why God attends to humans; Psalm 19 sees creation and instruction address humans in different ways.

rightEvidence.title: Creation and instruction disclose God differently

compares.tension: Humans are both small within creation and responsible hearers of God’s disclosed order.
compares.title: Human vocation beneath speaking heavens

leftEvidence.title: The absent God becomes the God of praise

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The speaker addresses God as absent and silent, remembers earlier trust, asks for rescue, and anticipates praise among nations and future generations.
points.right: The LORD is named as shepherd who provides, restores, guides, accompanies through death-shadow, hosts, anoints, and gives enduring welcome.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Lament moves through mockery and danger toward testimony and communal worship.
points.right: The speaker shifts from speaking about God to speaking directly to God in the darkest valley.

compares.posture: Psalm 22 cries over abandonment; Psalm 23 speaks directly to God’s presence in death-shadow.

rightEvidence.title: The LORD shepherds through danger

compares.tension: Both prayers keep God as their addressee while naming opposite experiences of presence.
compares.title: The God addressed as absent and present

leftEvidence.title: God is asked to cleanse and recreate

points.label: Divine action
points.left: God is addressed as merciful judge who can wash, create a clean heart, renew a spirit, restore joy, and receive truthful sacrifice.
points.right: The LORD forgives, heals, rescues, judges for the oppressed, reveals ways to Moses, shows compassion, and remembers human dust.

points.label: Human response
points.left: The speaker confesses, asks not to lose God’s presence, and promises teaching and praise.
points.right: The speaker commands self, angels, works, and all places to bless the LORD.

compares.posture: Psalm 51 asks God to recreate the guilty speaker; Psalm 103 praises God’s compassion toward frail creatures.

rightEvidence.title: God’s mercy is measured against human frailty

compares.tension: Confession depends on mercy without treating guilt as mere weakness or weakness as guilt.
compares.title: A clean heart and remembered dust

leftEvidence.title: God knows, surrounds, and examines

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The LORD knows speech and movement, is present across height and depth, forms life in the womb, and is invited to search the speaker.
points.right: God is said to make everything fitting in its time, place eternity in human hearts, give work and enjoyment, and act enduringly.

points.label: Human response
points.left: The speaker moves from wonder and attempted escape to hatred of enemies and a request for examination.
points.right: Humans experience opposite seasons but cannot discover the whole work from beginning to end.

compares.posture: Psalm 139 speaks of God’s complete knowledge of a person; Ecclesiastes describes people unable to grasp God’s whole work.

rightEvidence.title: God gives time and limits human grasp

compares.tension: The human is fully known while remaining a limited knower.
compares.title: Known completely, unable to know the whole

leftEvidence.title: The Holy One commissions Isaiah

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The Lord sits high on a throne, is acclaimed as holy, shakes the thresholds, cleanses Isaiah, and asks whom to send.
points.right: The LORD measures creation, has no instructor or equal, rules nations, names the stars, and gives strength to the weary.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Isaiah confesses unclean lips, receives cleansing, hears the question, and volunteers.
points.right: Exiles who say their way is hidden are called to look, know, wait, and renew strength.

compares.posture: Isaiah’s call begins in a throne vision; the exile oracle develops God’s incomparability through creation and care.

rightEvidence.title: God is incomparable and attends the weary

compares.tension: Overwhelming holiness and strength for the weary belong to the same prophetic witness.
compares.title: The Holy One enthroned and the Creator without equal

leftEvidence.title: God calls Cyrus without being known by him

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The LORD calls Cyrus anointed, subdues nations, names and equips him, declares sole deity, and claims light, darkness, well-being, and calamity.
points.right: The LORD calls the wicked to return for abundant pardon and compares the divine word to rain that accomplishes its purpose.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Cyrus acts as an instrument before he knows the God who names him.
points.right: Seekers must turn; hearers are told that God’s thoughts and ways exceed theirs.

compares.posture: Cyrus acts within a purpose he does not know; the rain-like word accomplishes the purpose for which God sends it.

rightEvidence.title: God’s higher ways and effective word

compares.tension: Divine purpose works through both human political action and proclaimed speech without erasing their differences.
compares.title: A named ruler and a word that succeeds

leftEvidence.title: God rejects confidence in the temple

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The LORD commands amended ways, condemns oppression and idolatry, and warns that the house bearing the divine name can be treated like Shiloh.
points.right: The LORD promises a new covenant unlike the broken exodus covenant, writes instruction on hearts, renews belonging, spreads knowledge, and forgives sin.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Worshipers repeat “the LORD’s temple” while committing injustice and trusting the building.
points.right: The houses of Israel and Judah receive a restored relation not sustained by external teaching alone.

compares.posture: Jeremiah rejects trust in a building bearing God’s name and later promises instruction written within.

rightEvidence.title: God promises instruction written within

compares.tension: External sacred identity is exposed when justice fails; renewed covenant reaches the heart without becoming private only.
compares.title: A named house and an inwardly written covenant

leftEvidence.title: Glory appears in human likeness and fire

points.label: Divine action
points.left: Above the living beings and platform, Ezekiel sees a throne, a human-like figure, fire, brightness, and rainbow likeness called the LORD’s glory.
points.right: The Lord GOD says restoration is not for Israel’s sake, sanctifies the profaned name, gathers, cleanses, gives a new heart and Spirit, and produces obedience.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Ezekiel falls on his face and hears a voice.
points.right: Israel is restored and then remembers its ways with shame.

compares.posture: Ezekiel’s vision uses layers of likeness; the restoration oracle explains action through the profaned and sanctified name.

rightEvidence.title: God acts for the holy name and renews Israel

compares.tension: God is disclosed through both a guarded vision and public action among nations.
compares.title: Guarded glory and the sanctified name

leftEvidence.title: God breathes life into dry bones

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The LORD interprets the bones as Israel, commands prophecy, reunites bodies, gives breath, opens graves, and promises the Spirit and land.
points.right: The Ancient of Days sits in fiery judgment, the court opens books, beasts lose dominion, and one like a son of man receives everlasting rule.

points.label: Human response
points.left: The prophet speaks as commanded; the hopeless house receives a new future.
points.right: Heavenly attendants serve; the human-like figure approaches and receives the nations.

compares.posture: Ezekiel sees national life restored through breath and Spirit; Daniel sees everlasting rule granted after imperial judgment.

rightEvidence.title: The Ancient of Days gives dominion

compares.tension: The future is pictured through renewed people in one vision and a human-like ruler in the other.
compares.title: Life by the Spirit and dominion from the throne

leftEvidence.title: God’s compassion interrupts destruction

points.label: Divine action
points.left: God recalls loving and teaching Israel, names their refusal, asks how to give them up, and says compassion grows warm.
points.right: The LORD’s day is warned as darkness, festivals and songs are rejected, and justice and righteousness are demanded like flowing water.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Israel sacrifices to Baals and bends away, yet will later follow when the LORD roars.
points.right: The people desire the LORD’s day and maintain worship while justice is absent.

compares.posture: Hosea voices God’s compassion within betrayed parenthood; Amos rejects worship that refuses public justice.

rightEvidence.title: God rejects worship without justice

compares.tension: Divine mercy does not make injustice irrelevant, and divine judgment does not silence compassion.
compares.title: Compassion that recoils and justice that rolls

leftEvidence.title: God’s case narrows extravagant worship to faithful life

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The prophetic exchange rejects escalating offerings as the answer and recalls what the LORD requires: justice, mercy, and humble walking with God.
points.right: The prophet portrays God coming in splendor and judgment, remembers mighty acts, trembles, and chooses joy even when fields fail.

points.label: Human response
points.left: The worshiper imagines costly gifts, even a firstborn, before the familiar requirement is stated.
points.right: Fear and bodily weakness give way to waiting and rejoicing in the God of salvation.

compares.posture: Micah names ordinary covenant faithfulness; Habakkuk portrays trust when ordinary provision disappears.

rightEvidence.title: God’s terrifying advent becomes the ground of trust

compares.tension: Life with God includes both active justice and patient joy under conditions humans cannot fix.
compares.title: Walking humbly and waiting through loss

leftEvidence.title: God returns to dwell in a truthful city

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The LORD expresses jealous concern for Zion, promises to return, renames Jerusalem by truth and holiness, gathers people, and renews covenant belonging.
points.right: The LORD announces a messenger and sudden coming, compares the arrival to refining fire, purifies worship, judges oppression, and grounds survival in divine constancy.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Old and young fill the streets; scattered people become God’s people.
points.right: Priests and people face purification; vulnerable people’s treatment becomes evidence in judgment.

compares.posture: Zechariah promises divine return to a renewed city; Malachi grounds purification and survival in divine constancy.

rightEvidence.title: The unchanging God comes to refine and judge

compares.tension: Return names changed covenant conditions, while constancy names the God who brings that change.
compares.title: God returns and God does not change

leftEvidence.title: God is named in Jesus’ conception and mission

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The child is conceived from the Holy Spirit, named Jesus because he will save his people from sins, and identified through Isaiah’s “God with us.”
points.right: Jesus is baptized, heaven opens, God’s Spirit descends, and a heavenly voice names the beloved Son and delight.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Joseph receives the angelic message, obeys, takes Mary, and names the child.
points.right: John objects and then consents; Jesus comes out of the water and receives the signs.

compares.posture: Matthew first interprets Jesus as God with us, then distinguishes Jesus, the Spirit, and the heavenly voice at baptism.

rightEvidence.title: Father, Son, and Spirit appear at baptism

compares.tension: Divine presence is centered in Jesus without collapsing the Father, Son, and Spirit into one speaker.
compares.title: God with us and the beloved Son

leftEvidence.title: Jesus teaches prayer to the Father

points.label: Divine action
points.left: Jesus directs disciples to a Father who knows needs, gives a shared prayer, and ties received and extended forgiveness together.
points.right: Jesus addresses the Father as Lord of heaven and earth, says mutual knowledge belongs uniquely to Father and Son, and invites the weary to himself.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Disciples pray privately and communally for God’s name, kingdom, will, provision, forgiveness, and deliverance.
points.right: Things are hidden from the wise, revealed to infants, and mediated through the Son.

compares.posture: Jesus teaches ordinary prayer to the Father and then claims unique mutual knowledge between Father and Son.

rightEvidence.title: Jesus thanks the Father and offers rest

compares.tension: The Father is directly addressed by disciples yet known through the Son’s revelation.
compares.title: The Father who hears and the Son who reveals

leftEvidence.title: The voice identifies the beloved Son

points.label: Divine action
points.left: A bright cloud overshadows Jesus, Moses, and Elijah; the voice repeats beloved Son language and commands the disciples to listen to him.
points.right: Jesus addresses “my God” in abandonment, cries again, dies, and is followed by torn curtain, earthquake, opened tombs, and the centurion’s confession.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Jesus shines; Peter proposes three shelters; the disciples fall afraid and later see Jesus alone.
points.right: Bystanders misunderstand the cry; the centurion and guards fear and name Jesus God’s Son.

compares.posture: The mountain voice names the beloved Son; at the cross the Son cries to “my God” in abandonment.

rightEvidence.title: Jesus cries to God and dies

compares.tension: Public affirmation and felt abandonment stand within the same Gospel’s account of Father and Son.
compares.title: The Father’s delight and the Son’s abandonment cry

leftEvidence.title: Jesus commissions in one shared name

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The risen Jesus claims all authority, sends disciples to all nations, commands baptism in the singular name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and promises presence.
points.right: The prologue distinguishes the Word as with God, calls the Word God, attributes creation and life to him, and says the Word became flesh and made the unseen God known.

points.label: Human response
points.left: The disciples worship and some doubt; they receive a teaching and baptizing mission.
points.right: Witnesses receive or reject the light; believers become God’s children.

compares.posture: Matthew closes with one name of Father, Son, and Spirit; John opens with the Word both with God and called God.

rightEvidence.title: The Word is with God and is God

compares.tension: Both texts compress distinction and divine identity without offering a later technical explanation.
compares.title: The shared baptismal name and the Word who reveals God

leftEvidence.title: God loves and sends the Son

points.label: Divine action
points.left: God’s love gives the only Son for life, sends him not to condemn but to save, while judgment appears through response to light.
points.right: Jesus says the Father works, the Son sees and does the Father’s works, gives life, receives judgment authority, and is to be honored as the Father.

points.label: Human response
points.left: People either believe and come to light or love darkness because their works are evil.
points.right: Opponents hear equality with God; hearers must honor and believe.

compares.posture: John 3 emphasizes God’s loving sending; John 5 emphasizes works, life, judgment, and honor shared with the Son.

rightEvidence.title: The Son does what the Father does

compares.tension: The Son is sent in saving purpose and also exercises authority associated with the Father.
compares.title: The sent Son and the Son who gives life

leftEvidence.title: Jesus says “I am” before Abraham

points.label: Divine action
points.left: Jesus honors the Father, promises life to those keeping his word, and closes the dispute by saying, “Before Abraham came into existence, I am.”
points.right: Jesus describes shared keeping of the sheep, says he and the Father are one, and defends his claim through works and Scripture.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Opponents accuse, question, invoke Abraham, and pick up stones.
points.right: Opponents seek a direct answer, attempt stoning for blasphemy, and try to arrest him.

compares.posture: Two disputes turn on Jesus’ relation to Abraham, the Father, and divine identity language.

rightEvidence.title: Jesus says he and the Father are one

compares.tension: Jesus distinguishes himself from the Father while making claims his opponents hear as blasphemous equality.
compares.title: “I am” and “the Father and I are one”

leftEvidence.title: Seeing Jesus is tied to seeing the Father

points.label: Divine action
points.left: Jesus names himself as way, truth, and life, says knowing him means knowing the Father, and speaks of mutual indwelling through words and works.
points.right: Jesus addresses the Father, speaks of shared glory before the world, gives eternal life through knowing Father and Son, and asks for protected, sanctified unity.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Philip asks to see the Father; Jesus directs attention to his own presence and works.
points.right: Disciples are given words and sent; future believers are included in the prayer.

compares.posture: Jesus tells Philip that seeing him discloses the Father, then directly addresses the Father in prayer.

rightEvidence.title: Jesus prays to the Father about glory and unity

compares.tension: Revelatory unity and personal distinction both remain explicit.
compares.title: Seeing the Father and speaking to the Father

leftEvidence.title: Thomas addresses Jesus as Lord and God

points.label: Divine action
points.left: The risen Jesus offers Thomas the requested wounds and calls him from unbelief to belief.
points.right: Wind, fire, languages, and prophetic speech mark the Spirit’s arrival, which Peter interprets through God’s promise to pour out the Spirit on all kinds of people.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Thomas answers, “My Lord and my God”; later readers are invited to believe without seeing.
points.right: The gathered disciples speak; the crowd hears, wonders, and disputes what the sign means.

compares.posture: John ends its signs with Thomas addressing Jesus as God; Acts begins public mission with God’s Spirit poured out through the exalted Jesus’ promise.

rightEvidence.title: God pours out the Spirit

compares.tension: Worship of the risen Jesus and the gift of the Spirit both direct attention to God’s action after resurrection.
compares.title: Thomas’s confession and God’s poured-out Spirit

leftEvidence.title: Paul names the unknown God as creator and judge

points.label: Divine action
points.left: Paul identifies the creator as Lord of heaven and earth, giver of life, near to all, commander of repentance, and appointed judge through a raised man.
points.right: God’s power and deity are said to be perceptible in created things, while truth is suppressed and the Creator is exchanged for images.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Athenians worship without knowing, search for God, and hear a resurrection claim.
points.right: Humans know, refuse gratitude, become futile, and worship created things.

compares.posture: Paul’s Athenian speech and Romans 1 both begin from creation while addressing different audiences and responses.

rightEvidence.title: God is known through creation and exchanged for images

compares.tension: One speech seeks repentance from incomplete worship; the letter describes truth suppressed and the Creator exchanged.
compares.title: The Creator proclaimed and the Creator exchanged

leftEvidence.title: God works through groaning toward glory

points.label: Divine action
points.left: God subjects creation in hope, gives the Spirit to help weakness, works toward good for the called, justifies, and anchors inseparable love in Christ.
points.right: Paul denies real standing to idols and names one God, the Father, as source and goal, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, as agent of creation and life.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Creation, believers, and the Spirit groan; believers wait, pray, suffer, and hope.
points.right: Believers exist from and for God and through the Lord amid a world of claimed gods and lords.

compares.posture: Romans anchors assurance in God’s purpose and love in Christ; Corinthians reshapes the one-God confession around Father and Jesus.

rightEvidence.title: One God and one Lord reshape divine identity

compares.tension: Divine action for believers and divine identity language meet without erasing Father-Son distinction.
compares.title: God for us and the one Lord through whom we exist

leftEvidence.title: God exalts the one in God’s form

points.label: Divine action
points.left: Christ Jesus is described in God’s form, taking slave form, obeying to death, and then being highly exalted by God so every tongue confesses him Lord.
points.right: God speaks through a Son who made the worlds, bears divine glory and imprint, sustains all things, makes purification, and is addressed in royal and divine language.

points.label: Human response
points.left: The community is called to the same mind; every knee and tongue responds to Jesus to God the Father’s glory.
points.right: Angels worship and serve; the Son sits at God’s right hand and exceeds them.

compares.posture: Philippians follows Christ from divine form through humiliation to exaltation; Hebrews begins from radiance, imprint, creation, and enthronement.

rightEvidence.title: God speaks in the Son, the exact imprint

compares.tension: One text stresses self-lowering and bestowed exaltation; the other stresses sustaining glory and inherited superiority.
compares.title: God’s form and God’s exact imprint

leftEvidence.title: God’s unseen love becomes visible among people

points.label: Divine action
points.left: God is called love, sends the Son, gives the Spirit, and makes abiding love visible through mutual love and confession.
points.right: The enthroned one announces God’s dwelling, the end of death and tears, final judgment, free water of life, and a city lit by God and the Lamb.

points.label: Human response
points.left: Believers love because God loved first; fear is displaced by mature love.
points.right: Peoples become God’s people, servants see God’s face, and nations walk by the city’s light.

compares.posture: First John locates unseen God’s visibility in sent Son, given Spirit, confession, and mutual love; Revelation pictures face-to-face dwelling.

rightEvidence.title: God dwells with humanity and makes all things new

compares.tension: Present mediated visibility and final direct presence belong to one trajectory but are not the same experience.
compares.title: God’s love made visible and God’s dwelling made complete

edges.basis: The two creation scenes move from God’s ordering speech to the human vocation created within that ordered world. God alone creates, while humans receive a derived image and delegated rule.
edges.label: Creator and image bearers

edges.basis: The planted place is first given as life-giving provision and later guarded after human disobedience. The same God gives breath and trees, then clothes the humans and bars access to the tree of life.
edges.label: Gifted garden and guarded garden

edges.basis: Cain’s murder and the flood generation show divine attention to bloodshed at personal and world scale. Cain receives judgment and protection; the corrupt earth receives judgment through the flood with one family preserved.
edges.label: Violence seen in one life and in the earth

edges.basis: The post-flood covenant secures creation’s continuance, while Babel shows that preservation does not remove divine judgment of human ambition. God promises not to repeat the flood yet still intervenes against a unified city project.
edges.label: A preserved earth and a scattered city

edges.basis: The initial call promises blessing; the later vision specifies descendants, land, delay, and affliction. A broad promise to bless the families of earth develops through one family’s long and painful future.
edges.label: Called blessing and delayed covenant

edges.basis: One scene marks Abraham’s household; the other lets Abraham question how the Judge of all the earth treats righteous and wicked. Belonging is marked bodily, while justice is explored through sustained dialogue.
edges.label: Covenant sign and covenant justice

edges.basis: The Isaac test threatens the promised line; Jacob’s dream renews the promise to a fugitive descendant. God tests one bearer of promise and assures another without explaining why their encounters differ so sharply.
edges.label: The threatened promise and promised presence

edges.basis: Jacob names a direct, wounding encounter with God; Joseph names God’s purpose within human actions across years. One scene is immediate and mysterious; the other interprets providence after events have unfolded.
edges.label: God in struggle and behind survival

edges.basis: Moses receives the divine name at the bush; Israel receives a chain of actions through which that name will be known. The name is spoken before deliverance and then tied to what God promises to do.
edges.label: The disclosed name and promised acts

edges.basis: The two scenes preserve distinct acts of deliverance from the same Egyptian crisis. One protects marked houses amid death; the other opens a public path and closes it over pursuers.
edges.label: Rescue through blood and through water

edges.basis: The mountain appearance prepares for the direct covenant words that follow. Dangerous nearness and moral instruction belong together, yet the people end at a distance.
edges.label: God descends and God speaks

edges.basis: Moses’ appeal after the calf is followed by God’s own proclamation of mercy, faithfulness, forgiveness, and judgment. The narrative says God relents; the proclamation refuses to reduce mercy to the absence of accountability.
edges.label: Intercession and the proclaimed character

edges.basis: The completed dwelling is filled by glory, and priestly service culminates in fire from before the LORD. Both signs confirm presence while also producing distance, awe, and bodily response.
edges.label: Presence that fills and fire that accepts

edges.basis: Atonement regulates entrance and removal of sin; blessing places God’s name and peace on the people. The people are brought near through priestly mediation that includes both costly cleansing and generous speech.
edges.label: Guarded approach and named blessing

edges.basis: God supplies leadership through the Spirit and later confronts a people who refuse trust despite signs. Divine provision widens participation, while persistent unbelief still brings consequence after pardon.
edges.label: Shared Spirit and resisted presence

edges.basis: Meribah identifies leaders who fail to sanctify God; the Shema calls the whole people to exclusive love and remembered words. God gives water even as leaders fail, while covenant loyalty is framed as a daily whole-life response.
edges.label: Failed sanctification and whole-person love

edges.basis: Joshua begins with assurance tied to instruction; Judges narrates repeated abandonment after that generation. God’s presence and covenant words remain, while Israel’s response cycles through forgetting, oppression, and rescue.
edges.label: Promised presence and recurring abandonment

edges.basis: Samuel becomes a prophet through hearing God, then later hears Israel demand visible rule like the nations. God establishes prophetic speech and also permits a kingship request named as rejection.
edges.label: A heard voice and a demanded king

edges.basis: The promise to David reverses his building plan; Solomon later prays at the completed temple without confining God there. Dynasty and sanctuary are both connected to God yet neither becomes possession or containment.
edges.label: God promises a house and hears from a house

edges.basis: Carmel gives a public answer by fire; Horeb corrects Elijah through a quieter encounter and a hidden remnant. God’s action is unmistakable in one scene and easily overlooked in the other.
edges.label: Fire before the nation and a quiet word to Elijah

edges.basis: Naaman comes to confess Israel’s God through healing; Assyria’s king mocks that God and is driven back. Nations encounter God through mercy in one scene and judgment in the other.
edges.label: God known by a foreigner and challenged by an empire

edges.basis: Chronicles explains exile through rejected messengers; Job’s losses begin through a heavenly exchange hidden from the sufferer. One history gives a moral sequence; the other denies the sufferer access to the scene behind his pain.
edges.label: Public judgment and hidden heavenly permission

edges.basis: Job 38 displays divine knowledge through creation questions; Psalm 82 displays divine authority through judgment of exalted rulers. God’s unmatched perspective does not remove the demand that delegated powers practice justice.
edges.label: The Creator questions Job and judges the assembly

edges.basis: Wisdom describes powerful mercy through God’s care for creatures; Sirach says speech cannot finish naming God’s greatness. Specific claims about mercy coexist with confession that God exceeds human praise.
edges.label: Measured mercy and praise beyond speech

edges.basis: Psalm 8 asks why God attends to humans; Psalm 19 sees creation and instruction address humans in different ways. Humans are both small within creation and responsible hearers of God’s disclosed order.
edges.label: Human vocation beneath speaking heavens

edges.basis: Psalm 22 cries over abandonment; Psalm 23 speaks directly to God’s presence in death-shadow. Both prayers keep God as their addressee while naming opposite experiences of presence.
edges.label: The God addressed as absent and present

edges.basis: Psalm 51 asks God to recreate the guilty speaker; Psalm 103 praises God’s compassion toward frail creatures. Confession depends on mercy without treating guilt as mere weakness or weakness as guilt.
edges.label: A clean heart and remembered dust

edges.basis: Psalm 139 speaks of God’s complete knowledge of a person; Ecclesiastes describes people unable to grasp God’s whole work. The human is fully known while remaining a limited knower.
edges.label: Known completely, unable to know the whole

edges.basis: Isaiah’s call begins in a throne vision; the exile oracle develops God’s incomparability through creation and care. Overwhelming holiness and strength for the weary belong to the same prophetic witness.
edges.label: The Holy One enthroned and the Creator without equal

edges.basis: Cyrus acts within a purpose he does not know; the rain-like word accomplishes the purpose for which God sends it. Divine purpose works through both human political action and proclaimed speech without erasing their differences.
edges.label: A named ruler and a word that succeeds

edges.basis: Jeremiah rejects trust in a building bearing God’s name and later promises instruction written within. External sacred identity is exposed when justice fails; renewed covenant reaches the heart without becoming private only.
edges.label: A named house and an inwardly written covenant

edges.basis: Ezekiel’s vision uses layers of likeness; the restoration oracle explains action through the profaned and sanctified name. God is disclosed through both a guarded vision and public action among nations.
edges.label: Guarded glory and the sanctified name

edges.basis: Ezekiel sees national life restored through breath and Spirit; Daniel sees everlasting rule granted after imperial judgment. The future is pictured through renewed people in one vision and a human-like ruler in the other.
edges.label: Life by the Spirit and dominion from the throne

edges.basis: Hosea voices God’s compassion within betrayed parenthood; Amos rejects worship that refuses public justice. Divine mercy does not make injustice irrelevant, and divine judgment does not silence compassion.
edges.label: Compassion that recoils and justice that rolls

edges.basis: Micah names ordinary covenant faithfulness; Habakkuk portrays trust when ordinary provision disappears. Life with God includes both active justice and patient joy under conditions humans cannot fix.
edges.label: Walking humbly and waiting through loss

edges.basis: Zechariah promises divine return to a renewed city; Malachi grounds purification and survival in divine constancy. Return names changed covenant conditions, while constancy names the God who brings that change.
edges.label: God returns and God does not change

edges.basis: Matthew first interprets Jesus as God with us, then distinguishes Jesus, the Spirit, and the heavenly voice at baptism. Divine presence is centered in Jesus without collapsing the Father, Son, and Spirit into one speaker.
edges.label: God with us and the beloved Son

edges.basis: Jesus teaches ordinary prayer to the Father and then claims unique mutual knowledge between Father and Son. The Father is directly addressed by disciples yet known through the Son’s revelation.
edges.label: The Father who hears and the Son who reveals

edges.basis: The mountain voice names the beloved Son; at the cross the Son cries to “my God” in abandonment. Public affirmation and felt abandonment stand within the same Gospel’s account of Father and Son.
edges.label: The Father’s delight and the Son’s abandonment cry

edges.basis: Matthew closes with one name of Father, Son, and Spirit; John opens with the Word both with God and called God. Both texts compress distinction and divine identity without offering a later technical explanation.
edges.label: The shared baptismal name and the Word who reveals God

edges.basis: John 3 emphasizes God’s loving sending; John 5 emphasizes works, life, judgment, and honor shared with the Son. The Son is sent in saving purpose and also exercises authority associated with the Father.
edges.label: The sent Son and the Son who gives life

edges.basis: Two disputes turn on Jesus’ relation to Abraham, the Father, and divine identity language. Jesus distinguishes himself from the Father while making claims his opponents hear as blasphemous equality.
edges.label: “I am” and “the Father and I are one”

edges.basis: Jesus tells Philip that seeing him discloses the Father, then directly addresses the Father in prayer. Revelatory unity and personal distinction both remain explicit.
edges.label: Seeing the Father and speaking to the Father

edges.basis: John ends its signs with Thomas addressing Jesus as God; Acts begins public mission with God’s Spirit poured out through the exalted Jesus’ promise. Worship of the risen Jesus and the gift of the Spirit both direct attention to God’s action after resurrection.
edges.label: Thomas’s confession and God’s poured-out Spirit

edges.basis: Paul’s Athenian speech and Romans 1 both begin from creation while addressing different audiences and responses. One speech seeks repentance from incomplete worship; the letter describes truth suppressed and the Creator exchanged.
edges.label: The Creator proclaimed and the Creator exchanged

edges.basis: Romans anchors assurance in God’s purpose and love in Christ; Corinthians reshapes the one-God confession around Father and Jesus. Divine action for believers and divine identity language meet without erasing Father-Son distinction.
edges.label: God for us and the one Lord through whom we exist

edges.basis: Philippians follows Christ from divine form through humiliation to exaltation; Hebrews begins from radiance, imprint, creation, and enthronement. One text stresses self-lowering and bestowed exaltation; the other stresses sustaining glory and inherited superiority.
edges.label: God’s form and God’s exact imprint

edges.basis: First John locates unseen God’s visibility in sent Son, given Spirit, confession, and mutual love; Revelation pictures face-to-face dwelling. Present mediated visibility and final direct presence belong to one trajectory but are not the same experience.
edges.label: God’s love made visible and God’s dwelling made complete

topic.orientation: Follow what Scripture says God does, says, permits, promises, judges, gives, and leaves unexplained. Keep poetry, narrative, law, prophecy, Gospel, letter, and vision distinct while tracing the relationships among God, Jesus, the Spirit, people, creation, and the nations.

pivots.description: God creates, addresses human beings, judges violence, preserves life, and limits human ambition.

nodes.note: God creates the heavens and earth, speaks light into darkness, and names day and night.
nodes.title: God creates and speaks light

nodes.note: God deliberates, makes humankind in the divine image, blesses them, and gives them rule and food.
nodes.title: God makes humanity in God’s image

nodes.note: The LORD God forms the man from dust, breathes life, plants a garden, and causes trees to grow.
nodes.title: God forms and plants

nodes.note: God calls to the hiding humans, questions them, announces consequences, clothes them, and bars the tree of life.
nodes.title: God seeks, questions, judges, and clothes

nodes.note: God questions Cain, warns about sin, names Abel’s blood as a witness, judges Cain, and marks him against vengeance.
nodes.title: God warns Cain and hears blood

nodes.note: God sees pervasive evil, grieves, announces destruction, and gives Noah detailed instructions for preservation.
nodes.title: God grieves violence and preserves Noah

nodes.note: God receives Noah’s offering, promises not to strike every living thing again, blesses life, and gives the rainbow as covenant sign.
nodes.title: God limits judgment and sets the bow

nodes.note: The LORD comes down, assesses the city and tower, confuses speech, and scatters the builders.
nodes.title: God descends and scatters Babel

pivots.title: Maker and the early world

pivots.description: God calls, promises, tests, meets, wrestles, and works through family histories.

nodes.note: The LORD commands Abram to leave and promises land, nation, blessing, and a wider blessing through him.
nodes.title: God calls Abram away

nodes.note: God answers Abram’s fear and childlessness, counts faith as righteousness, and binds the land promise through a covenant sign.
nodes.title: God promises descendants and land

nodes.note: God identifies himself as God Almighty, renames Abram, promises descendants and land, and commands circumcision.
nodes.title: God names covenant and sign

nodes.note: The LORD chooses to disclose the outcry against Sodom and allows Abraham’s repeated appeal concerning the righteous and wicked.
nodes.title: God discloses judgment to Abraham

nodes.note: God commands the offering of Isaac, stops Abraham’s hand, provides a ram, and renews the promise.
nodes.title: God tests Abraham over Isaac

nodes.note: The LORD stands above the stairway, repeats the ancestral promise, and promises presence and return.
nodes.title: God meets Jacob in flight

nodes.note: A mysterious man wrestles Jacob, wounds him, renames him Israel, and blesses him.
nodes.title: God meets Jacob in struggle

nodes.note: Joseph distinguishes his brothers’ evil intention from God’s intention to preserve many lives.
nodes.title: Joseph names God’s purpose in human evil

pivots.title: Promise and the patriarchs

pivots.description: God names himself, hears Israel, confronts Egypt, gives covenant words, and discloses mercy and judgment.

nodes.note: God appears in fire, declares Israel’s suffering seen and heard, commissions Moses, and gives the name tied to “I AM.”
nodes.title: God hears and names himself

nodes.note: God names himself as the LORD and promises to bring out, redeem, take Israel as a people, and bring them into the land.
nodes.title: God links the name to covenant action

nodes.note: The LORD strikes Egypt’s firstborn while the marked Israelite houses are passed over.
nodes.title: God passes through Egypt

nodes.note: The LORD commands movement, divides the sea, protects Israel, throws Egypt into confusion, and returns the waters.
nodes.title: God makes a path through the sea

nodes.note: God names Israel a treasured possession and priestly kingdom, sets boundaries, and descends in fire, cloud, sound, and trembling.
nodes.title: God descends on Sinai

nodes.note: God identifies himself as deliverer, forbids rival gods and images, and orders worship, time, family, life, marriage, property, speech, and desire.
nodes.title: God speaks covenant commands

nodes.note: God tells Moses of Israel’s corruption, announces consuming wrath, and relents after Moses appeals to reputation and promise.
nodes.title: God threatens judgment and relents

nodes.note: The LORD passes before Moses and proclaims mercy, grace, patience, covenant love, faithfulness, forgiveness, and judgment.
nodes.title: God proclaims the divine name and character

pivots.title: Name and deliverance

pivots.description: Glory, holiness, atonement, blessing, Spirit, rebellion, and loyalty shape life near God.

nodes.note: The cloud covers the tent, the LORD’s glory fills it, and the cloud or fire directs Israel’s journeys.
nodes.title: Glory fills the tabernacle

nodes.note: The LORD’s glory appears and fire consumes the offering on the altar.
nodes.title: Fire comes from before the LORD

nodes.note: The LORD regulates Aaron’s entrance, offerings, incense, blood, and the two goats for atonement and removal of sins.
nodes.title: God provides guarded approach and removal

nodes.note: The LORD gives words by which priests place the divine name on Israel: blessing, keeping, light, grace, attention, and peace.
nodes.title: God places the name in blessing

nodes.note: The LORD takes from the Spirit on Moses and places it on seventy elders, including two who remain in the camp.
nodes.title: God shares the Spirit among elders

nodes.note: The LORD charges Israel with unbelief, threatens destruction, hears Moses’ appeal, pardons, and still bars the rebellious generation from the land.
nodes.title: God judges unbelief and hears intercession

nodes.note: The LORD instructs Moses to speak to the rock, gives water, and says Moses and Aaron failed to believe and sanctify him.
nodes.title: God gives water and judges leaders

nodes.note: The command names the LORD as Israel’s God, calls for whole-person love, and places the words through daily life.
nodes.title: Israel hears that the LORD is one

pivots.title: Presence in the wilderness

pivots.description: God accompanies Israel, speaks through prophets, answers prayer, and challenges royal power.

nodes.note: The LORD promises presence, land, and success tied to courage and careful attention to the instruction.
nodes.title: God commissions Joshua

nodes.note: The LORD’s anger gives Israel into enemies, mercy raises judges, and judgment tests the nations when Israel repeatedly turns away.
nodes.title: God responds to Israel’s recurring abandonment

nodes.note: The LORD calls Samuel, confirms judgment on Eli’s house, and establishes Samuel as a trustworthy prophet.
nodes.title: God calls Samuel in a time of rare words

nodes.note: The LORD tells Samuel that Israel has rejected divine kingship, orders a warning, and finally tells him to appoint a king.
nodes.title: God interprets Israel’s demand for a king

nodes.note: The LORD recalls moving in a tent, rejects David’s proposed temple role, and promises David a house, son, kingdom, and enduring throne.
nodes.title: God refuses David’s house and promises one

nodes.note: Solomon praises covenant faithfulness and asks God to hear prayers directed toward the temple across sin, defeat, drought, exile, and foreign prayer.
nodes.title: Solomon addresses the God heaven cannot contain

nodes.note: The LORD answers Elijah’s prayer with fire that consumes offering, wood, stones, dust, and water.
nodes.title: God answers Elijah by fire

nodes.note: The LORD questions Elijah, passes by amid wind, earthquake, and fire, speaks in a low sound, and gives new assignments and a preserved remnant.
nodes.title: God questions Elijah and speaks after the storm

pivots.title: Land, judges, and kings

pivots.description: Foreigners, empires, heavenly assemblies, wisdom, judgment, and mercy widen the field.

nodes.note: The God of Israel heals Naaman through Elisha’s simple instruction and receives the foreigner’s confession.
nodes.title: God heals a foreign commander

nodes.note: The LORD is addressed as creator and enthroned God, answers the Assyrian boast, promises Jerusalem’s deliverance, and strikes the camp.
nodes.title: God answers Assyria’s challenge

nodes.note: The God of the ancestors repeatedly sends messengers, gives the people over after sustained rejection, and later stirs Cyrus to rebuild.
nodes.title: God warns, judges, and stirs return

nodes.note: God commends Job and sets limits on the accuser’s power while permitting devastating loss.
nodes.title: God permits Job’s testing in the heavenly court

nodes.note: The LORD questions Job about earth, sea, dawn, death, and the world’s breadth rather than first explaining Job’s suffering.
nodes.title: God answers Job from the whirlwind

nodes.note: God stands in an assembly, rebukes unjust rulers called gods, and announces that they will die like humans.
nodes.title: God judges in the divine assembly

nodes.note: The writer says God can act with great power yet orders all things by measure and shows mercy because all belong to God.
nodes.title: God’s power is described through measure and mercy

nodes.note: The sage says human speech cannot finish naming God, whose works exceed praise and whose greatness is beyond tracing.
nodes.title: Praise reaches the limit of speech

pivots.title: Judgment, exile, and the nations

pivots.description: Poetry speaks to and about God through praise, grief, confession, trust, knowledge, and time.

nodes.note: The psalm addresses the LORD’s majestic name, recalls the heavens as divine work, and marvels that God remembers and appoints humans.
nodes.title: God’s majesty and human vocation

nodes.note: The heavens declare God’s glory without audible speech, while the LORD’s instruction speaks clearly, restores, warns, and exposes hidden faults.
nodes.title: Creation and instruction disclose God differently

nodes.note: The speaker addresses God as absent and silent, remembers earlier trust, asks for rescue, and anticipates praise among nations and future generations.
nodes.title: The absent God becomes the God of praise

nodes.note: The LORD is named as shepherd who provides, restores, guides, accompanies through death-shadow, hosts, anoints, and gives enduring welcome.
nodes.title: The LORD shepherds through danger

nodes.note: God is addressed as merciful judge who can wash, create a clean heart, renew a spirit, restore joy, and receive truthful sacrifice.
nodes.title: God is asked to cleanse and recreate

nodes.note: The LORD forgives, heals, rescues, judges for the oppressed, reveals ways to Moses, shows compassion, and remembers human dust.
nodes.title: God’s mercy is measured against human frailty

nodes.note: The LORD knows speech and movement, is present across height and depth, forms life in the womb, and is invited to search the speaker.
nodes.title: God knows, surrounds, and examines

nodes.note: God is said to make everything fitting in its time, place eternity in human hearts, give work and enjoyment, and act enduringly.
nodes.title: God gives time and limits human grasp

pivots.title: Prayer and wisdom

pivots.description: Prophets encounter holiness, announce judgment, name God’s purposes, and hold out renewal.

nodes.note: The Lord sits high on a throne, is acclaimed as holy, shakes the thresholds, cleanses Isaiah, and asks whom to send.
nodes.title: The Holy One commissions Isaiah

nodes.note: The LORD measures creation, has no instructor or equal, rules nations, names the stars, and gives strength to the weary.
nodes.title: God is incomparable and attends the weary

nodes.note: The LORD calls Cyrus anointed, subdues nations, names and equips him, declares sole deity, and claims light, darkness, well-being, and calamity.
nodes.title: God calls Cyrus without being known by him

nodes.note: The LORD calls the wicked to return for abundant pardon and compares the divine word to rain that accomplishes its purpose.
nodes.title: God’s higher ways and effective word

nodes.note: The LORD commands amended ways, condemns oppression and idolatry, and warns that the house bearing the divine name can be treated like Shiloh.
nodes.title: God rejects confidence in the temple

nodes.note: The LORD promises a new covenant unlike the broken exodus covenant, writes instruction on hearts, renews belonging, spreads knowledge, and forgives sin.
nodes.title: God promises instruction written within

nodes.note: Above the living beings and platform, Ezekiel sees a throne, a human-like figure, fire, brightness, and rainbow likeness called the LORD’s glory.
nodes.title: Glory appears in human likeness and fire

nodes.note: The Lord GOD says restoration is not for Israel’s sake, sanctifies the profaned name, gathers, cleanses, gives a new heart and Spirit, and produces obedience.
nodes.title: God acts for the holy name and renews Israel

pivots.title: The prophetic voice

pivots.description: Spirit, kingship, compassion, justice, waiting, restoration, and divine constancy face the future.

nodes.note: The LORD interprets the bones as Israel, commands prophecy, reunites bodies, gives breath, opens graves, and promises the Spirit and land.
nodes.title: God breathes life into dry bones

nodes.note: The Ancient of Days sits in fiery judgment, the court opens books, beasts lose dominion, and one like a son of man receives everlasting rule.
nodes.title: The Ancient of Days gives dominion

nodes.note: God recalls loving and teaching Israel, names their refusal, asks how to give them up, and says compassion grows warm.
nodes.title: God’s compassion interrupts destruction

nodes.note: The LORD’s day is warned as darkness, festivals and songs are rejected, and justice and righteousness are demanded like flowing water.
nodes.title: God rejects worship without justice

nodes.note: The prophetic exchange rejects escalating offerings as the answer and recalls what the LORD requires: justice, mercy, and humble walking with God.
nodes.title: God’s case narrows extravagant worship to faithful life

nodes.note: The prophet portrays God coming in splendor and judgment, remembers mighty acts, trembles, and chooses joy even when fields fail.
nodes.title: God’s terrifying advent becomes the ground of trust

nodes.note: The LORD expresses jealous concern for Zion, promises to return, renames Jerusalem by truth and holiness, gathers people, and renews covenant belonging.
nodes.title: God returns to dwell in a truthful city

nodes.note: The LORD announces a messenger and sudden coming, compares the arrival to refining fire, purifies worship, judges oppression, and grounds survival in divine constancy.
nodes.title: The unchanging God comes to refine and judge

nodes.note: The child is conceived from the Holy Spirit, named Jesus because he will save his people from sins, and identified through Isaiah’s “God with us.”
nodes.title: God is named in Jesus’ conception and mission

nodes.title: Father, Son, and Spirit appear at baptism

nodes.note: Jesus directs disciples to a Father who knows needs, gives a shared prayer, and ties received and extended forgiveness together.
nodes.title: Jesus teaches prayer to the Father

nodes.note: Jesus addresses the Father as Lord of heaven and earth, says mutual knowledge belongs uniquely to Father and Son, and invites the weary to himself.
nodes.title: Jesus thanks the Father and offers rest

nodes.note: A bright cloud overshadows Jesus, Moses, and Elijah; the voice repeats beloved Son language and commands the disciples to listen to him.
nodes.title: The voice identifies the beloved Son

nodes.note: Jesus addresses “my God” in abandonment, cries again, dies, and is followed by torn curtain, earthquake, opened tombs, and the centurion’s confession.
nodes.title: Jesus cries to God and dies

nodes.note: The risen Jesus claims all authority, sends disciples to all nations, commands baptism in the singular name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and promises presence.
nodes.title: Jesus commissions in one shared name

nodes.note: The prologue distinguishes the Word as with God, calls the Word God, attributes creation and life to him, and says the Word became flesh and made the unseen God known.
nodes.title: The Word is with God and is God

pivots.title: Jesus names the Father

nodes.title: God loves and sends the Son

nodes.title: The Son does what the Father does

nodes.title: Jesus says “I am” before Abraham

nodes.note: Jesus describes shared keeping of the sheep, says he and the Father are one, and defends his claim through works and Scripture.
nodes.title: Jesus says he and the Father are one

nodes.note: Jesus names himself as way, truth, and life, says knowing him means knowing the Father, and speaks of mutual indwelling through words and works.
nodes.title: Seeing Jesus is tied to seeing the Father

nodes.note: Jesus addresses the Father, speaks of shared glory before the world, gives eternal life through knowing Father and Son, and asks for protected, sanctified unity.
nodes.title: Jesus prays to the Father about glory and unity

nodes.note: The risen Jesus offers Thomas the requested wounds and calls him from unbelief to belief.
nodes.title: Thomas addresses Jesus as Lord and God

nodes.note: Wind, fire, languages, and prophetic speech mark the Spirit’s arrival, which Peter interprets through God’s promise to pour out the Spirit on all kinds of people.
nodes.title: God pours out the Spirit

nodes.title: God works through groaning toward glory

nodes.title: One God and one Lord reshape divine identity

nodes.note: Christ Jesus is described in God’s form, taking slave form, obeying to death, and then being highly exalted by God so every tongue confesses him Lord.
nodes.title: God exalts the one in God’s form

nodes.note: God speaks through a Son who made the worlds, bears divine glory and imprint, sustains all things, makes purification, and is addressed in royal and divine language.
nodes.title: God speaks in the Son, the exact imprint

nodes.note: God is called love, sends the Son, gives the Spirit, and makes abiding love visible through mutual love and confession.
nodes.title: God’s unseen love becomes visible among people
